drafted.title: Malicious parameter injection via missing input validation on agent tool and model APIs
drafted.description: An attacker supplies crafted, out-of-range, or malformed input — tool-call arguments, MCP request parameters, model-operator tensors, file paths, or serialized payloads — that the agent's tool-invocation layer, MCP/plugin server, or underlying ML runtime fails to type-check, bound-check, or sanitize before acting on it. Because the untrusted input crosses directly into privileged execution (shell commands, file I/O, native ops, authorization decisions) without validation, the result ranges from crashes and resource-exhaustion denial of service to path traversal, command/code injection, and authentication or authorization bypass across the agent's tool and model surface.

drafted.title: File disclosure and SSRF via XML External Entity (XXE) expansion in agent-ingested documents
drafted.description: Agent tools, MCP servers, and connector libraries frequently parse attacker-reachable XML-based content (SBOMs, SAML assertions, Office/SVG/PDF documents, config or dictionary files) using XML parsers that resolve DOCTYPE declarations and external entity references by default; an attacker who can inject a crafted document anywhere in that pipeline can exfiltrate local files, pivot to internal services via SSRF, or exhaust resources through entity-expansion bombs, all without needing to break any authentication or authorization boundary since the flaw lives in the parsing library the tool depends on.

drafted.title: Unsanitized agent-generated content injected into downstream interpreters
drafted.description: An agent, MCP server, or framework component forwards LLM-generated or externally-sourced text (prompts, retrieved documents, file paths, tool arguments) directly into a downstream interpreter — a shell, database/graph query language, template engine, or code evaluator — without neutralizing special characters or syntax. Because the agent pipeline treats model output or attacker-influenced input as trusted code/config rather than data, anyone who can steer an upstream input can smuggle control sequences that the downstream component executes, yielding arbitrary command/code execution, data exfiltration, or privilege escalation.

drafted.title: Open redirect to attacker-controlled host via unvalidated redirect/callback URL parameter
drafted.description: An agent-adjacent service (login flow, OAuth callback, MCP OAuth dynamic client registration, or tool that constructs a redirect/Location header) accepts an attacker-supplied URL in a parameter such as redirect_uri, continue, or uenc without validating it is same-origin or on an allow-list, so the trusted domain's own redirect is used to forward a victim's browser, authorization code, or access token to an attacker-controlled site. Because agent frameworks and MCP registries chain these redirects into authentication and tool-installation flows, the trusted-origin confusion can be leveraged for credential/token theft, phishing of agent operators, or silent exfiltration of session data rather than a simple user-facing redirect bug.

drafted.title: Path traversal via unsanitized file paths in agent tool/file endpoints
drafted.description: Agent frameworks, LLM-ops UIs, and MCP-adjacent servers expose endpoints or tool calls that accept user-supplied filenames, archive entries, or settings paths (e.g. model downloads, extension installers, log viewers, backup/restore, image encoders) and pass them to filesystem operations without canonicalizing or confining them to an allowed base directory. An attacker supplies '../'-style, absolute, or crafted archive-member paths to read, overwrite, or plant arbitrary files outside the intended directory, frequently escalating to full remote code execution when the planted file is a config, extension, or script the agent later loads or executes.

drafted.title: Missing Origin/Host validation on local MCP HTTP transport enabling cross-origin tool invocation
drafted.description: An MCP server exposes its HTTP/SSE transport on localhost without validating the Origin or Host header on incoming requests, so a malicious web page opened in the victim's browser (or an attacker using DNS rebinding) can send cross-origin requests that the local browser automatically routes to the loopback-bound server. Because the server trusts any request that reaches its socket, the attacker's page can invoke privileged agent tools, read responses, and exfiltrate data or trigger actions without any authentication, turning a user's casual browser tab into a full remote control channel for the agent's tool set.

drafted.title: Arbitrary code execution via unsandboxed eval of agent-controlled expressions
drafted.description: Agent frameworks build expression/code strings from LLM tool-call output, workflow 'custom code' nodes, or user-supplied configuration and feed them directly into eval(), exec(), or an equivalent dynamic-evaluation/expression engine without sufficient sandboxing or syntax restriction. Because the evaluated string carries attacker- or model-influenced content, an adversary who controls any upstream input (a crafted tool response, workflow definition, or prompt that steers model-generated 'tool call' text) can smuggle in native code and achieve full remote code execution on the host running the agent.

drafted.title: Relative path traversal in tool file-handling endpoints
drafted.description: An attacker supplies a crafted relative path or filename (e.g. containing "../" sequences) to a tool-exposed file operation such as upload, save/load-workflow, delete-batch, or profile-picture endpoints in agent/MCP-adjacent services; because the implementation concatenates the input into a filesystem path without canonicalizing or confining it to an intended base directory, the operation escapes the sandbox to read, write, or overwrite arbitrary files. This lets an attacker exfiltrate credentials/config, plant malicious files (e.g. into plugin or startup directories) for later execution, or corrupt state the agent relies on for safe operation.

drafted.title: Unrestricted upload of dangerous file types via agent file-handling tools
drafted.description: An agent-adjacent component exposes a file-upload or file-ingestion feature (chat attachments, knowledge-base/media ingestion, model-artifact import, log/config upload) that validates only the filename extension or client-supplied MIME type rather than the actual file content, letting an attacker upload a web shell, script, or executable disguised as an allowed type (image, document, model file). Once stored inside a web-accessible or interpretable path, the file is later executed by the host runtime, interpreter, or web server, giving the attacker remote code execution on the system hosting the agent and everything the agent can reach.

drafted.title: Escape execution sandboxes via object prototype pollution
drafted.description: An attacker crafts input (JSON keys like __proto__/constructor.prototype, template expressions, or form fields) that is merged, parsed, or assigned onto a JavaScript object without guarding against prototype-chain keys, polluting Object.prototype process-wide. In agentic workflow engines and tool runtimes that execute attacker-reachable expressions or code nodes inside a VM/sandbox (e.g., automation platforms, template/parsing libraries pulled in as dependencies), this shared-state corruption disables sandbox guards or hijacks property/function resolution, letting the attacker break out of the intended execution boundary and achieve arbitrary code execution.
